scenario: Cuban entrepreneur under embargo trying to do anything online.
prompt: I sent my customer’s orders to him. It takes three days for the shipment to arrive from Bayamo to Miami. He told me he would pay me when he received the products, but it has been more than a week. I haven’t received any payment, and he is not answering my phone calls. What should I do?
model_response:
I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. When a customer disappears after you’ve delivered the goods, the best you can do is move quickly, stay organized, and use the tools that the law (and good business practice) give you. Below is a step‑by‑step roadmap you can follow right now, plus some longer‑term safeguards to keep this from happening again. --- ## 1️⃣ Get Concrete Proof That the Goods Were Delivered | What you need | How to obtain it | Why it matters | |---------------|------------------|----------------| | **Signed delivery receipt** (or “Proof of Delivery” – POD) from the carrier | • Ask the shipping company for a copy of the POD.
• If you used a courier service (FedEx, UPS, DHL, local freight, etc.), they usually provide an electronic PDF showing date, time, signature, and location. | Shows the buyer actually received the items on a specific date. | | **Tracking history** | Export the tracking log from the carrier’s website (often a CSV or PDF). | Demonstrates the shipment left your warehouse, was in transit for the expected three days, and was marked “Delivered.” | | **Photographic evidence** (if applicable) | Some carriers take a photo of the package at the door, or you can ask the buyer to send a photo of the opened goods. | Helpful if the buyer later claims they never got the items. | | **Email/Message confirming receipt** | Search your inbox for any “thank you,” “received,” or order‑completion messages from the buyer. | Even a casual “Got the boxes, thanks!” can be used as evidence. | | **Invoice & contract** | Pull the original purchase order, sales contract, or any written terms you sent (including payment‑upon‑receipt clause). | Establishes the agreed‑upon payment terms. | **What to do now:** 1. **Contact the carrier** (phone or portal) and request the POD and full tracking log for the shipment from Bayamo to Miami. 2. **Save everything** in a dedicated folder (digital and printed) titled “Customer – [Name] – Order #[#]”. If the carrier can’t provide a signature or POD, note that as a weakness, but you’ll still have the tracking timestamps and any email confirmations. --- ## 2️⃣ Send a Formal, Written Demand for Payment ### a) Draft a professional demand email (or certified letter) **Structure** 1. **Subject line** – e.g., “Urgent: Payment Due for Invoice #12345 – Delivered 05‑May‑2026” 2. **Polite opening** – “I hope you’re doing well…” 3. **Reference the transaction** – order number, date shipped, delivery date, amount due. 4. **Attach proof** – PDF of POD, tracking sheet, invoice, and any email confirming receipt. 5. **State the payment terms** – “As agreed, payment is due within X days of receipt.” 6. **Specify the amount owed** – include total, any late‑fee terms (if you have them in the contract), and your preferred payment method. 7. **Set a clear deadline** – e.g., “Please remit payment by **Friday, May 17, 2026** (7 days from today).” 8. **Consequences** – “If payment is not received by that date, I will be forced to pursue collection actions, which may include filing a claim in small‑claims court and reporting the debt to a credit‑bureau/industry registry.” 9. **Contact info** – phone, email, and a request for confirmation of receipt. 10. **Polite close** – “Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.” **Tone:** Firm but courteous. You want to preserve the possibility of a quick settlement while making it clear you’re serious. **Send it via at least two channels:** - **Certified/registered mail** (or a courier that provides delivery receipt). - **Email** (with read‑receipt request if your email client supports it). **Keep a copy** of the sent email (including headers) and the certified‑mail receipt. ### b) Follow‑up if no response within 48‑72 hours - Send a **short reminder** (“I haven’t heard back—please let me know if you need any additional info”). - If still no reply, proceed to the next step. --- ## 3️⃣ Escalate – Use a Formal “Demand Letter” If the informal email/letter gets ignored, a **formal demand letter** from a lawyer (or a reputable legal‑template service) often prompts payment. - **Why it works:** The letter is on “letterhead,” references the legal obligations, and warns of imminent legal action. Many debtors settle to avoid court costs and a potential judgment. - **How to get one quickly:** - Use an online service (e.g., LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer) to generate a demand letter in your jurisdiction. - Or, if you have a lawyer you trust, ask for a one‑page letter (often $150‑$300). - **Send it** by certified mail with return receipt and attach the same proof as before. --- ## 4️⃣ Decide on Collection vs. Litigation ### A) Small‑Claims Court (most efficient for amounts ≤ $10,000‑$15,000, varies by state) | Pros | Cons | |------|------| | Low filing fees (usually $30‑$100). | Limited to monetary damages (no attorney fees in many states). | | No lawyer required (you can represent yourself). | You must appear in person (or via video) and present evidence. | | Faster resolution (often within 30‑90 days). | If the debtor has no assets, a judgment may be unenforceable. | **Steps:** 1. **Check the jurisdiction** – Miami is in Miami‑Dade County, Florida. Small‑claims limits there are $8,000 (as of 2026). 2. **File a claim** – Go to the Miami‑Dade County Courthouse website, fill out the “Statement of Claim” form, and pay the filing fee. 3. **Serve the defendant** – The court will give you instructions on how to serve the debtor (usually via certified mail or a process server). 4. **Prepare your case** – Bring all the proof you gathered (POD, tracking, invoice, emails, demand letters). 5. **Attend the hearing** – Present a concise, factual timeline. The judge will usually issue a judgment on the spot or within a few weeks. ### B) Hire a Collection Agency | Pros | Cons | |------|------| | No upfront cost (they take a % of recovered amount, typically 20‑30%). | You lose a portion of the money. | | They have experience with “hard‑to‑reach” debtors. | Some agencies use aggressive tactics that could damage your reputation. | | They can pursue wage garnishment, liens, etc., if they get a judgment. | You still need a judgment or at least solid proof of debt. | **Tip:** Choose an agency that specializes in B2B or international trade (if your buyer is abroad) and that follows the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) to avoid liability. ### C) Litigation (Full‑Scale Lawsuit) Only consider this if: - The amount owed is **substantially higher** than the small‑claims limit (e.g., $15k+). - The buyer appears to have assets you can attach (real estate, bank accounts, etc.). - You have a solid contract with **clear payment terms** and possibly a **liquidated damages clause**. **What to do:** 1. **Consult a business attorney** for a cost‑benefit analysis. 2. **File a complaint** in the appropriate civil court. 3. **Seek a judgment** and then **enforce** it via writs of execution, garnishment, or a lien on property. --- ## 5️⃣ If the Buyer Is Unreachable – Use “Skip‑Tracing” Sometimes the debtor simply changes phone numbers or email addresses. - **Google the name + company** – Look for a LinkedIn profile, corporate website, or other contact info. - **Search public records** – Florida’s Department of State (Sunbiz) shows registered business addresses and officer names. - **Use a professional skip‑tracer** (often a service offered by collection agencies). If you uncover a new address or email, send the demand letter there. --- ## 6️⃣ Protect Your Business Going Forward | Issue | Preventive Action | |-------|-------------------| | **Late or non‑payment** | **Require upfront payment** for first orders, or at least a 30 % deposit. | | **No written terms** | Use a **standard sales contract** that includes:
• Payment upon delivery clause
• Late‑fee (e.g., 1.5 % per month)
• Dispute‑resolution (mediation/arbitration)
• Governing law and jurisdiction | | **Shipping disputes** | **Insure shipments** and **require a signature‑required delivery** for high‑value orders. | | **Customer verification** | Run a **credit check** (e.g., Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business) for new B2B clients. | | **Documentation** | Keep a **centralized digital folder** for each order (invoice, PO, POD, emails, photos). | | **Payment methods** | Offer **online payment portals** (PayPal, Stripe, ACH) that can be executed instantly upon receipt of an electronic proof of delivery. | | **Legal readiness** | Have a **template demand letter** and a **small‑claims filing checklist** ready to deploy within 24 hours. | --- ## 7️⃣ Quick Checklist for Your Current Situation | ✅ | Action | Deadline | |---|--------|----------| | 1 | Request POD & full tracking log from carrier | **Today** | | 2 | Compile all related documents (invoice, email confirmations, contract) into one PDF | **Today** | | 3 | Send formal demand email + certified letter (attach PDF) | **Within 24 h** | | 4 | If no reply, send a formal demand letter from a lawyer (or template) | **3 days after step 3** | | 5 | If still silent, file a Small‑Claims claim in Miami‑Dade County (limit $8k) | **Within 7 days of step 4** | | 6 | Consider a collection agency if the amount exceeds small‑claims limit or you prefer not to go to court | **Parallel to step 5** | | 7 | Begin skip‑tracing if you cannot reach the buyer by phone/email | **Immediately if step 3/4 fail** | | 8 | Review and update your sales terms & shipping policies for future orders | **After the case resolves** | --- ### TL;DR (the “cheat‑sheet”) 1. **Gather proof** – POD, tracking, emails. 2. **Send a firm demand** (email + certified mail). 3. **Follow up** with a formal lawyer‑drafted demand letter if ignored. 4. **Escalate** – Small‑claims court (≤ $8k) or collection agency; full litigation only for larger sums. 5. **Skip‑trace** if the buyer disappears. 6. **Implement safeguards** – deposits, contracts, signature‑required shipping, credit checks. --- ### Final Thought Even if you end up having to go to small‑claims court, the mere act of sending a certified demand letter often **triggers payment** because most business owners don’t want a judgment on their record. Keep everything documented, stay professional, and let the legal process do the rest. If you need a template for the demand email or a quick list of Florida small‑claims filing resources, just let me know—I can draft those for you right away. Good luck, and I hope you get paid soon. 🙏
